approachQuestion.prompt: Count the ways to choose indices from source s in increasing order so that their characters spell target t. Different index selections count separately, even if they spell the same text. Return the count modulo 1000000007. Examples: s="aaa", t="aa" → 3; s="abc", t="ac" → 1; s="ab", t="ba" → 0. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 1 ≤ n=s.length,m=t.length ≤ 1500; lowercase letters; inputs are read-only. Return only the modular count.

options.text: Keep m+1 counts, with count[0]=1. Scan source characters left to right. For each source character scan target positions j=m..1 downward; when it matches t[j−1], add count[j−1] into count[j] modulo the modulus. Return count[m].
options.feedback: The new source index is either omitted or matched to the last target character of a prefix. Descending target positions prevent this one source index from matching several target positions in the same pass.

options.text: Store counts for every source prefix and every target prefix, using the preceding source row for both omission and matching.
options.feedback: This computes the correct result on the whole domain, but retains old states that future transitions never read. Removing those states preserves correctness and reduces auxiliary storage.

options.text: Update target positions from 1 upward for each source character.
options.feedback: For s="a", t="aa", this reuses the same source index and returns one, although no legal selection exists.

options.text: Deduplicate identical source letters before counting their matches.
options.feedback: For s="aaa", t="aa", the three index pairs are distinct; deduplication loses them and can even make the target impossible.

feedback.reason: Count target embeddings by source indices while using descending updates to forbid index reuse.
details: Allocate m+1 counters, seed count[0]=1, and for each of n source characters inspect all m target positions downward. Do not stop early when m>n. Use index comparisons and modular word additions only.
Update target positions downward so one source character cannot satisfy two target positions in the same iteration. Equal source characters at different indices still create distinct subsequences.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Allocate m+1 counters, seed count[0]=1, and for each of n source characters inspect all m target positions downward. Do not stop early when m>n. Use index comparisons and modular word additions only. Analyze this fixed implementation. N=n+m; n,m vary independently. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.
Include initialization; treat the stated dimensions as variable parameters within their bounds. Use a word per stored counter or flag, not a packed bitset.

feedback.reason: Inspect all n*m pairs using one m+1 modular-count array.
details: All nm source/target comparisons occur. A single array of m+1 counters is retained. No index lists, substrings, hashes, recursion, or copies are allocated.
“O(n+m) time, O(m) auxiliary space”: Each of n source characters scans all m target positions, so there are nm comparisons.
“O(nm) time, O(nm) auxiliary space”: Descending updates let one target-prefix row replace all source-prefix rows.
“O(nm) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The method retains m+1 target-prefix counts, not just a single answer count.
